Q: Goaccess - Log format not working when invoked inside a bash script A:

Re-posting comment as an answer since formatting is important for the suggested change:

++++++++++++++++++++++++++=

I don't work with goaccess so I'm just guessing at this point ... cat ... | while read spawns a subshell for the while read loop, so the goaccess is being run in a subshell.

I'm guessing goaccess is missing something in the subshell; consider eliminating the subshell with a small change to your code.

The following should eliminate the subshell and allow the goaccess calls to be made in the current shell:

while read d ; do
    # echo "goaccess /var/log/httpd/www.$d/access_log --log-format=COMBINED -o /srv/www/parked-domains/mystats/www.$d/index.html"

    ## uncomment previous line to output each invocation of goaccess and
    ## comment the following line, otherwise bash script will terminate

    goaccess /var/log/httpd/www.$d/access_log --log-format=COMBINED -o /srv/www/parked-domains/mystats/www.$d/index.html
done < domainlist.txt

Q: GDB python API - getting the python API of gdb to print the offending line number A:

Catch the exception inside your script, at some proper position, and pretty print the exception and backtrace as you like.

I want to suggest you refer to some gdb plugin written in gdbpython, including peda, gef, pwndbg, etc. Such plugins have virtually used every feature of gdbpython, and contain very good practice for writing python gdb plugin. Robust gdbpython plugins usually have pretty-printer for python exceptions.

As an example, here is the backtrace pretty-printer of gef: (of course you cannot use it directly, since it contains too many gef internal functions)

def show_last_exception():
    """Display the last Python exception."""
    print("")
    exc_type, exc_value, exc_traceback = sys.exc_info()
    print(" Exception raised ".center(80, horizontal_line))
    print("{}: {}".format(Color.colorify(exc_type.__name__, attrs="bold underline red"), exc_value))
    print(" Detailed stacktrace ".center(80, horizontal_line))
    for fs in traceback.extract_tb(exc_traceback)[::-1]:
        if PYTHON_MAJOR==2:
            filename, lineno, method, code = fs
        else:
            filename, lineno, method, code = fs.filename, fs.lineno, fs.name, fs.line

        print("""{} File "{}", line {:d}, in {}()""".format(down_arrow, Color.yellowify(filename),
                                                            lineno, Color.greenify(method)))
        print("   {}    {}".format(right_arrow, code))

    print(" Last 10 GDB commands ".center(80, horizontal_line))
    gdb.execute("show commands")
    print(" Runtime environment ".center(80, horizontal_line))
    print("* GDB: {}".format(gdb.VERSION))
    print("* Python: {:d}.{:d}.{:d} - {:s}".format(sys.version_info.major, sys.version_info.minor,
                                                   sys.version_info.micro, sys.version_info.releaselevel))
    print("* OS: {:s} - {:s} ({:s}) on {:s}".format(platform.system(), platform.release(),
                                                    platform.architecture()[0],
                                                    " ".join(platform.dist())))
    print(horizontal_line*80)
    print("")
    return

Q: Does Duck DB support triggers? A:

DuckDB 2.0 will support triggers:

Triggers have been a long-standing feature request, and DuckDB v2.0 delivers them in full: BEFORE and AFTER triggers, FOR EACH ROW and FOR EACH STATEMENT, transition tables via REFERENCING OLD/NEW TABLE, multiple triggers per event, RETURNING on triggered tables, and DROP TRIGGER.

The classic use case is audit tables: something happens in the system, and a trigger records what changed. For example:

CREATE TRIGGER trg_audit AFTER UPDATE ON target
REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS o NEW TABLE AS n
FOR EACH STATEMENT
    INSERT INTO audit
    SELECT n.id, o.val, n.val
    FROM o
    JOIN n ON o.id = n.id;

Q: Is fetching std::chrono::steady_clock inside a critical section necessary to theoretically align C++ happens-before with real-time order? A:

The C++ memory model does not rely on real time.

Inverting physical time would indeed reverse causes and effects. But the C++ memory model does not encode physical causality — only logical visibility. Since happens‑before is not defined in terms of real time, reversing time does not affect it. The abstract machine has no temporal axis to invert.

Happens‑before is a logical ordering defined by synchronization primitives (mutexes, atomic fences, etc.).

A mutex enforces a strict order :

– thread A enters the critical section

– thread B waits

– thread B enters afterwards

This order is real, observable, and independent of physical time.

The standard does not require calling steady_clock::now() inside the critical section, because clocks have no role in the happens‑before relation.

In other words :

you can invert time, and the memory model stays exactly the same (apart from physical causes becoming physical consequences, et vice versa).

The mutex defines the ordering, not the clock.

And if we really want to be pedantic:

the C++ abstract machine is not temporally covariant, nor does it impose chrono‑causal constraints on synchronization semantics.

As CodeGuru Coluche would put it :

“Go faster, and time shrinks.”

Q: How to loop a function and save the outputs of each run as independent objects? A:

Use Map and assign the result to list L and then L$mpg etc can get individual components. Alternately use list2env to place the components of L into the global environment. Normally using a list is preferable to having loose objects in the global environment.

# 1
library(dplyr)
 
calculate_summary <- function(var) {
  mtcars %>% 
    dplyr::group_by(cyl, vs) %>% 
    dplyr::summarise(
      N = length(.data[[var]]),
      mean = mean(.data[[var]]),
      sd   = sd(.data[[var]]),
      se   = sd / sqrt(N),
      .groups = "drop")
}
 
L <- Map(calculate_summary, c("mpg", "qsec"))
L$mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 6
##     cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2     4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3     6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4     6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5     8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

or


# 2
list2env(L, globalenv())
<environment: R_GlobalEnv>

mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 6
##     cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2     4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3     6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4     6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5     8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

Another approach is to create a single data frame and then filter it:

# 3
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

DF <- map_dfr(set_names(c("mpg", "qsec")), calculate_summary, .id = "group")
filter(DF, group == "mpg")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##   group   cyl    vs     N  mean     sd     se
##   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1 mpg       4     0     1  26   NA     NA    
## 2 mpg       4     1    10  26.7  4.75   1.50 
## 3 mpg       6     0     3  20.6  0.751  0.433
## 4 mpg       6     1     4  19.1  1.63   0.816
## 5 mpg       8     0    14  15.1  2.56   0.684

If the last approach is of interest note that the dlookr package's describe function works with group_by eliminating calculate_summary.

# 4
library(dlookr)
library(dplyr)

DF2 <- mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl, vs) %>%
  describe(mpg, qsec, statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se_mean"))

filter(DF2, described_variables == "mpg")
## # A tibble: 5 × 8
##   described_variables   cyl    vs     n    na  mean     sd se_mean
##   <chr>               <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 mpg                     4     0     1     0  26   NA      NA    
## 2 mpg                     4     1    10     0  26.7  4.75    1.50 
## 3 mpg                     6     0     3     0  20.6  0.751   0.433
## 4 mpg                     6     1     4     0  19.1  1.63    0.816
## 5 mpg                     8     0    14     0  15.1  2.56    0.684

or to produce a list without calculate_summary add a split at the end:

# 5
library(dlookr)
library(dplyr)

L2 <- mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl, vs) %>%
  describe(mpg, qsec, statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se_mean")) %>%
  { split(.[-1], .[[1]]) }
L2$mpg
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##     cyl    vs     n    na  mean     sd se_mean
##   <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1     4     0     1     0  26   NA      NA    
## 2     4     1    10     0  26.7  4.75    1.50 
## 3     6     0     3     0  20.6  0.751   0.433
## 4     6     1     4     0  19.1  1.63    0.816
## 5     8     0    14     0  15.1  2.56    0.684

To add on to Nathan Roberts' answer, consider using f-strings like so:

Q: Scan directories and copy those that have more than n files A:

Since OP has commented - I haven't coded for 20 years - and has tagged the question with bash, I'll throw a (relatively) basic bash script into the mix.

First, create OP's sample directories/files:

rm -rf music*

mkdir -p music{,light}

mkdir -p music/artist{1..3}

mkdir -p music/artist1/album{1..3}
touch music/artist1/album1/1-1-1.txt
touch music/artist1/album2/1-2-{1..2}.txt
touch music/artist1/album3/1-3-{1..6}.txt

mkdir -p music/artist2/album1
touch music/artist2/album1/2-1-1.txt

mkdir -p music/artist3/album{1..2}
touch music/artist3/album1/3-1-1.txt
touch music/artist3/album2/3-2-{1..2}.txt

Result:

$ tree
├── music
│   ├── artist1
│   │   ├── album1
│   │   │   └── 1-1-1.txt
│   │   ├── album2
│   │   │   ├── 1-2-1.txt
│   │   │   └── 1-2-2.txt
│   │   └── album3
│   │       ├── 1-3-1.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-2.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-3.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-4.txt
│   │       ├── 1-3-5.txt
│   │       └── 1-3-6.txt
│   ├── artist2
│   │   └── album1
│   │       └── 2-1-1.txt
│   └── artist3
│       ├── album1
│       │   └── 3-1-1.txt
│       └── album2
│           ├── 3-2-1.txt
│           └── 3-2-2.txt
├── musiclight

11 directories, 15 files

General design:

  • use find / type -d to obtain a list of artists (directories)
  • for each artist use find / type -f to obtain a list of songs (files) under the artist's directory
  • to get around potential issues with file names containing linefeeds or control characters we'll have find just print a 1 (ie, we don't care about file names at this point so we just need something simple we can count)
  • use wc -l to count the results of the 2nd find (ie, the number of songs/files)
  • if the count is greater-than/equal to OP's threshold (eg, threshold=7) then recursively copy the artist's directory to the target directory

Putting all of this into bash code:

src='music'
tgt='musiclight'

threshold=7

while read -r artist
do
    [[ "${artist}" == "${src}" ]] && continue                  # ignore top most directory '${src}'

    song_count=$(find "${artist}" -type f -printf '1\n' | wc -l)

    if [[ "${song_count}" -ge "${threshold}" ]]
    then
        cp -rp "${artist}" "${tgt}"                            # recursively copy files, preserve mode/ownership/timestamps
    fi
done< <(find "${src}" -maxdepth 1 -type d)                     # get list of artists

Result for threshold=7:

$ tree musiclight
musiclight
└── artist1
    ├── album1
    │   └── 1-1-1.txt
    ├── album2
    │   ├── 1-2-1.txt
    │   └── 1-2-2.txt
    └── album3
        ├── 1-3-1.txt
        ├── 1-3-2.txt
        ├── 1-3-3.txt
        ├── 1-3-4.txt
        ├── 1-3-5.txt
        └── 1-3-6.txt

4 directories, 9 files

Result for threshold=3:

$ tree musiclight
musiclight
├── artist1
│   ├── album1
│   │   └── 1-1-1.txt
│   ├── album2
│   │   ├── 1-2-1.txt
│   │   └── 1-2-2.txt
│   └── album3
│       ├── 1-3-1.txt
│       ├── 1-3-2.txt
│       ├── 1-3-3.txt
│       ├── 1-3-4.txt
│       ├── 1-3-5.txt
│       └── 1-3-6.txt
└── artist3
    ├── album1
    │   └── 3-1-1.txt
    └── album2
        ├── 3-2-1.txt
        └── 3-2-2.txt

7 directories, 12 files
